stimulus.text:
| Group | Response to the Declaration |
| African Americans | Its natural-rights language seemed to challenge slavery. Jefferson's first draft blamed slavery on Britain, but Congress removed that passage. Some enslaved people fled to the British; some in the North won freedom by serving in the militia or the Continental Army. |
| Native Americans | Most supported the British, fearing the land hunger of the new nation. |
| Women | Revolutionary ideals inspired the idea of republican motherhood: women would educate their sons to be citizens of the republic, so mothers themselves needed education. |

books.section: B. Common Sense, the Declaration of Independence, and Republican Self-Government

stem: Why did the Declaration of Independence give many enslaved African Americans hope?

options.text: Because Congress freed all enslaved people when it adopted the Declaration
options.misconception: Congress did not free anyone in 1776 — the Declaration freed no enslaved person, and slavery continued.

options.text: Because its natural-rights language seemed to challenge the institution of slavery
Because Jefferson's final draft blamed slavery on the British
options.misconception: Jefferson's blame of Britain was in his first draft, and Congress removed that passage before adoption.

options.text: Because the British promised freedom to every enslaved person in the colonies
options.misconception: Background: some enslaved people fled to the British, but no British promise covered every enslaved person in the colonies.

rationales.B: The Declaration's claim that all men are created equal and endowed with unalienable rights seemed to condemn slavery itself. The hope lay in the principle, even though no law followed it yet.
rationales.A: The Declaration freed no one. Slavery continued after 1776, which is why the hope was in the language, not in a law.
rationales.C: The blame passage was cut. The final Declaration does not blame Britain for slavery.
rationales.D: Some fled to British lines, but there was no British promise of freedom to every enslaved person.
rationales.general:
1. Read the Declaration's claim. All men are created equal, endowed with unalienable rights.
2. Ask what that claim implies for slavery. If the rights belong to all men, slavery contradicts them.
3. Name the hope. Not a law freeing anyone, but language that seemed to condemn the institution.
Remember: a principle can challenge an institution before any law does — the hope was in the words, not in an act.
